To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of two or six hyperthermal treatments to radiation therapy yields similar tumor responses, that the mean of the minimum temperatures achieved is a prognostic factor for local control, and that the number of hyperthermic treatments is not a prognostic parameter.

two or six hypertherapy treatments administered as adjuncts to radiation therapy yield comparable local tumor responses and that the number of hyperthermy treatments does not correlate with duration of local tumor control.
two or six hyperhyperthermia treatments are equally effective as adjuncts to radiation therapy for the treatment of superficially located recurrent or metastatic cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an effective and practical hyperthermia protocol that can be administered to patients with recurrent or metastatic cancer.
the use of hyperthermia as a local treatment modality for superficially located tumors.
the use of hyperthermia as a therapeutic modality for patients with superficially located malignancies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
two hyperthermia treatments are as effective as six in terms of local tumor control.

two hyperthermia treatments, given at 24-hr intervals, as an adjunct to external beam radiation therapy, is as effective in producing complete disappearance of all tumor and in achieving local control as are six treatments, given at approximately 48-hr intervals, when the minimum intratumor temperature achieved during hyperthermia is greater than 41 degrees to 42 degrees C.
two hyperthermia treatments are equivalent to six hyperthermia treatment in the context of this study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

two hyperthermia treatments given at the time of radiation initiation and one hyperthermia treatment given at the end of the radiation course are as effective as six hyperthermia sessions administered in conjunction with a standardized course of radiation therapy.
two hyperthermia treatments are sufficient to achieve a response rate similar to that achieved with six treatments, and that a single hyperthermia treatment is insufficient to achieve a response.
the number of hyperthermic treatments is of no importance, and the most important factor for the development of thermotolerant cells is the time between treatments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multiple hyperthermia treatments may not be necessary to achieve optimal tumor response when hyperthermia is administered in conjunction with radiation therapy.
multiple closely spaced hypertherapy treatments may not improve tumor responses.
the number of hyperthermias administered should not be the only factor in determining the effectiveness of a hyperthermia protocol.
